paragraphs: Running experiments repeatedly creates two connected challenges: deciding which alternative performs best and controlling false discoveries across the growing collection of tests. This paper combines those decisions in a framework that replaces successive A/B tests with successive multi-armed bandit problems, each aimed at identifying the best option.

The framework lets researchers monitor each experiment continuously. The authors define null hypotheses for these bandit problems and construct sequential p-values that remain valid during monitoring. They then connect individual experiments to an online false discovery rate procedure, using its rejection thresholds to set the confidence levels of the bandit algorithms.

This connection makes sampling efficiency and error control part of the same design. The paper reports sample optimality, high statistical power, and low false discovery rates at any point in time within its framework. Extensive simulations and an application to New Yorker Cartoon Caption contest data support the claims. The contribution concerns both how efficiently experiments gather evidence and how their conclusions remain controlled across an ongoing sequence.
neurips-2017-a-framework-for-multi-a-rme.tldr: The framework combines continuously monitored bandit experiments with online false discovery control to support efficient testing over time.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover an underlying signal from observations. A common solver, ADMM, repeatedly performs several updates, two of which can require their own iterative calculations. This paper accelerates those updates with two pretrained convolutional networks, removing the inner loops while retaining the surrounding ADMM procedure.

The first network is a conditional denoising autoencoder that supplies an implicit prior about the desired signal. Its behavior depends on data, following an empirical Bayesian approach. This is amortized inference: training prepares a reusable network for a calculation that would otherwise require repeated optimization. The second network approximates the matrix inversion needed by the least-squares update. Its training requires neither ground-truth signals nor measurements.

The two networks therefore address different computational obstacles: applying a difficult prior and carrying out a large matrix inversion. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate efficiency and accuracy relative to conventional ADMM with inner loops. The stated result supports learned replacements for expensive internal calculations; the inversion network is explicitly an approximation.
neurips-2017-an-inner-loop-free-solution.tldr: Two pretrained convolutional networks replace costly inner ADMM calculations, improving the efficiency of inverse-problem solving in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Many fairness criteria evaluate statistical relationships among predictions, protected attributes, features, and outcomes. This paper argues that these observational relationships have inherent limits: they cannot conclusively settle questions of discrimination. The issue concerns what the observed distribution can establish about fairness, even when that distribution is available.

The authors instead express discrimination through causal reasoning. This changes the central modeling question from choosing a statistical fairness criterion to deciding which assumptions to make about the process generating the data. Those assumptions become an explicit part of the fairness analysis, rather than leaving the analysis dependent only on observed associations.

The paper formalizes why and when observational criteria fail and identifies subtleties that become visible through the causal perspective. It also proposes causal non-discrimination criteria and algorithms that satisfy them. These contributions connect a conceptual account of discrimination to concrete learning procedures. Their meaning depends on the causal modeling assumptions adopted: the approach makes those assumptions central to evaluating what a fairness guarantee actually establishes.
neurips-2017-avoiding-discrimination-thr.tldr: The paper explains limits of observational fairness criteria and develops causal non-discrimination criteria with algorithms that satisfy them.

paragraphs: Density estimation learns how probability is distributed across possible observations. This paper studies Bayesian estimators that build their representation by adaptively dividing the sample space into regions. Because the partition can adapt, the method belongs to a nonparametric class rather than requiring one fixed density shape.

The theoretical analysis asks how quickly the posterior distribution concentrates as evidence accumulates. Under a suitable prior, the authors establish concentration rates and show that, in several special cases, those rates do not depend directly on the dimension of the problem. The restriction to special cases matters: the result is not a general claim that dimension never affects density estimation.

A second finding concerns adaptation to the unknown smoothness of the true density. The estimators can achieve an optimal convergence rate without imposing the artificial density conditions discussed in the abstract. Simulated datasets provide validation of the theory. Together, the results explain when adaptive partitioning can offer both statistical efficiency and flexibility without requiring smoothness to be specified in advance.
neurips-2017-convergence-rates-of-a-part.tldr: Adaptive Bayesian partition estimators achieve optimal convergence while adapting to unknown smoothness, with dimension-independent rates in several special cases.

paragraphs: A set has members but no meaningful ordering. For a learning task defined on a set, rearranging those members should therefore leave the relevant output unchanged. Deep Sets studies how to design models around this requirement, called permutation invariance, instead of beginning with a fixed-dimensional vector representation.

The paper's main theorem characterizes permutation-invariant objective functions by identifying a structured family to which they must belong. That characterization provides a mathematical basis for constructing a deep network architecture that operates on sets. The architecture connects the symmetry required by the task to the form of the model used to learn it.

The authors demonstrate the method on population statistic estimation, point cloud classification, set expansion, and outlier detection. These applications span supervised and unsupervised learning, illustrating the reach of the set-based formulation. The contribution combines a theoretical description of invariant functions with an architecture motivated by that description. Its stated experimental role is to demonstrate applicability across these tasks, rather than establish a universal performance ranking.
neurips-2017-deep-sets-23f1dc9f96.tldr: Deep Sets uses a characterization of permutation-invariant functions to design neural networks for learning directly from sets.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization fits a model by reducing its loss on training data. This paper studies algorithms that perform this optimization with differential privacy. Its central concern is achieving strong utility guarantees while reducing gradient complexity, meaning the amount of gradient computation needed by the algorithm.

For smooth convex and strongly convex losses, the authors give algorithms with optimal or nearly optimal utility bounds and lower gradient complexity than previous work. Their treatment includes settings with no regularizer and settings with smooth or nonsmooth regularization. They also address smooth convex problems where the number of features greatly exceeds the number of observations, again reducing gradient complexity while attaining the stated upper bound.

The final contribution extends expected excess empirical risk analysis from convex objectives to objectives satisfying the Polyak–Lojasiewicz condition. In that setting, the paper provides a tighter utility upper bound than the cited earlier result. These are guarantees for specified optimization settings: the broader scope comes from covering additional objective conditions while improving the computational requirements of private learning.
neurips-2017-differentially-private-empi.tldr: The paper reduces gradient complexity for private empirical risk minimization and extends utility guarantees to Polyak–Lojasiewicz objectives.

paragraphs: Mutual information quantifies statistical dependence and serves as a building block in tasks such as correlation mining and conditional independence testing. This paper addresses estimating it when observations include discrete values, continuous values, or variables that combine both kinds of behavior within one distribution.

A common estimation strategy calculates separate entropies for each variable and their joint distribution, then combines the three quantities. The difficulty is that these individual entropy quantities need not be well defined in general mixture spaces, even though mutual information itself remains well defined. The problem therefore lies in the usual route to estimation, rather than in the dependence quantity being sought.

The authors introduce an estimator designed for these mixed settings and prove its consistency. This gives an asymptotic basis for the estimate approaching the target quantity as sample information grows within the theoretical setting. They also report strong empirical performance. The contribution makes mutual information estimation applicable to mixed data without relying on the problematic three-entropy decomposition.
neurips-2017-estimating-mutual-informati.tldr: A consistent mutual information estimator handles discrete-continuous mixtures where the usual entropy-based calculation may be undefined.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent tokens as continuous vectors, but assigning each token its own full vector can require many parameters for large vocabularies. Hash embeddings reduce that burden by sharing a pool of embedding vectors across tokens while retaining a weighted representation for each token.

For a given token, hashing selects several vectors from the shared pool. A token-specific weight vector combines them into the final representation. This construction brings together ordinary learned embeddings and the hashing trick: both appear as special cases of the broader scheme. The resulting representation allows parameter sharing without reducing every token to just one hashed vector.

Experiments show that the approach handles vocabularies containing millions of tokens and uses only a fraction of the parameters required by regular embeddings. Across the evaluated tasks, models using hash embeddings achieve at least comparable performance. The method also removes the need to construct a dictionary before training or prune the vocabulary afterward, simplifying vocabulary handling alongside the reported parameter savings.
neurips-2017-hash-embeddings-for-efficie.tldr: Hash embeddings combine shared, hash-selected vectors with token-specific weights to represent large vocabularies with far fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Choosing useful sets of items often assumes that their payoff is already known. In recommendation and influence selection, however, feedback may arrive only after an action is taken. This paper models that situation as interactive submodular bandit optimization, where each round supplies a context, requires an action, and returns noisy utility feedback.

The proposed SM-UCB algorithm maintains an upper confidence estimate of the payoff. This supports a balance between gathering information and selecting actions that look valuable from existing evidence. The utility is modeled over context-action combinations, so an action's value is evaluated together with the context in which it occurs.

Under the stated kernel smoothness assumption involving a bounded RKHS norm, the authors establish regret of order square root of the number of rounds and asymptotic no-regret behavior. Thus, average accumulated regret vanishes in the analyzed setting. Experiments cover movie and news recommendation, influence maximization, and personalized summarization. Across these applications, the authors report consistent improvements over prior methods.
neurips-2017-interactive-submodular-band.tldr: SM-UCB learns unknown submodular payoffs through interaction, with conditional no-regret guarantees and reported gains across four applications.

paragraphs: Metric learning asks how to learn a useful notion of distance from data. This paper investigates its statistical foundations when the metric has low-dimensional structure or is sparse. The distinction matters because the dimension of the original feature representation and the effective dimension of the distance rule need not be the same.

The authors develop both upper and minimax lower bounds on generalization error. Upper bounds describe achievable error control, while minimax lower bounds characterize unavoidable difficulty across the considered problem class. They also quantify sample complexity in terms of feature-space dimension and the dimension or rank of the underlying metric, making the roles of those quantities explicit.

Another part of the analysis bounds how accurately the learned metric approximates the true generative metric. That addresses recovery of the underlying distance structure as well as generalization. The mathematical results also illuminate ordinal embedding, also called non-metric multidimensional scaling. The contribution is a set of theoretical guarantees linking structural assumptions, available data, predictive error, and metric recovery.
neurips-2017-learning-low-dimensional-me.tldr: The paper bounds generalization, sample complexity, and recovery accuracy for learning low-rank and sparse metrics.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating the centers of spherical Gaussian mixture components from a single pass through streaming data. It analyzes a streaming form of Lloyd's clustering heuristic, with guarantees that require sufficiently separated centers and a good initial estimate. An online PCA-based clustering procedure supplies that initialization.

Under the stated separation conditions, the center estimates are asymptotically optimal up to constants. The finite-sample analysis separates initialization bias, which decays polynomially with sample count, from a variance term that decreases at a nearly optimal rate. The algorithm also has asymptotically optimal per-step time proportional to dimension times component count, with space growing as that product times the logarithm of component count.

A remaining approximation error arises because Lloyd's hard assignments do not explicitly exploit the Gaussian distribution. The authors therefore also analyze streaming EM, which uses soft assignments and the Gaussian model. For two Gaussian components, this approach estimates the true means consistently, with nearly optimal error decay toward zero. That consistency result is specifically stated for the two-component setting.
neurips-2017-learning-mixture-of-gaussia.tldr: Streaming clustering learns separated Gaussian centers efficiently, while a two-component streaming EM result removes the hard-assignment approximation error.

paragraphs: Data augmentation expands training data through transformations intended to preserve labels. Experts can often specify individual transformations, but choosing useful sequences of them requires additional manual work. This paper automates that composition step by learning how to assemble user-provided transformations into augmentation sequences.

The method trains a generative sequence model using an adversarial approach and unlabeled data. It can work with arbitrary, nondeterministic transformation functions, and the authors report robustness to misspecified user input. Once learned, the transformation model can generate augmented data for an end discriminative model. This separates learning an augmentation procedure from training the eventual classifier.

Experiments cover both images and text. Relative to standard heuristic augmentation, the reported improvements are 4.0 accuracy points on CIFAR-10, 1.4 F1 points on ACE relation extraction, and 3.4 accuracy points on a medical imaging dataset using domain-specific operations. These results support learning compositions as a practical way to make better use of supplied transformation knowledge, with the gains tied to the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2017-learning-to-compose-domain-.tldr: An adversarial sequence model learns to compose user-specified data transformations, improving augmentation results on the evaluated image and text tasks.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent combines updates proposed by multiple workers. This paper asks what happens when some workers behave arbitrarily, a failure model called Byzantine behavior. Such behavior can arise from bugs, asynchronous communication, biased local data, or deliberate attempts to disrupt learning.

The authors consider a population of workers with up to a specified number behaving this way, without restricting parameter-space size or dimension. They first show that aggregation based on a linear combination of submitted vectors cannot tolerate even one Byzantine worker in their setting. This identifies a fundamental weakness in the aggregation step used by the approaches under discussion.

The paper then formulates a resilience property capturing requirements for convergence despite faulty workers and introduces Krum, an aggregation rule satisfying that property. The authors argue that it provides the first provably Byzantine-resilient algorithm for distributed SGD and also report experimental evaluations. The contribution links a failure result for linear aggregation to a constructive rule with a formal resilience guarantee.
neurips-2017-machine-learning-with-adver.tldr: Krum provides a formally resilient gradient aggregation rule for distributed SGD with Byzantine workers.

paragraphs: Quick Shift is an algorithm for finding modes and forming clusters. This paper studies the statistical reliability of those outputs: whether structures recovered from sampled observations correspond to the modes and clusters of the underlying distribution. Its contribution is theoretical analysis of an established algorithm.

The authors provide finite-sample consistency guarantees for both mode recovery and cluster recovery under mild distributional assumptions. Finite-sample guarantees address behavior with a limited collection of observations, while consistency connects recovery to increasing amounts of data. Treating modes and clusters separately matters because identifying a distribution's peaks and recovering its grouping structure are distinct recovery goals.

The paper then uses these results to construct a consistent modal regression algorithm, extending the analysis beyond the original clustering task. The same statistical foundations thus support both recovery of distributional structure and a regression procedure centered on modes. The guarantees remain conditional on the distributional assumptions stated by the authors; their significance is to establish a principled basis for recovery in that setting.
neurips-2017-on-the-consistency-of-quick.tldr: The paper establishes conditional consistency guarantees for Quick Shift's mode and cluster recovery and derives a consistent modal regression method.

paragraphs: The edge partition model extracts overlapping structure from binary matrices. Its gamma-process prior is intended to reduce the number of active latent components automatically. The authors find empirically that this shrinkage often works poorly, producing overfitted solutions despite the model's built-in mechanism for controlling complexity.

Their analysis of expected model intensity suggests that gamma priors on hyperparameters interfere with the internal gamma process. They propose two alternative constructions: CEPM constrains those gamma priors, while DEPM replaces them with Dirichlet priors. These changes target the interaction between layers of the model that appears to undermine shrinkage.

For DEPM, the authors can integrate out all model parameters, including the infinitely many gamma-process components. This yields an infinite version, IDEPM, with efficient collapsed Gibbs sampling. Experiments show effective shrinkage in the proposed models and report state-of-the-art IDEPM performance in generalization, link prediction, mixing efficiency, and convergence speed. The findings connect prior design to both complexity control and practical inference behavior.
neurips-2017-on-the-model-shrinkage-effe.tldr: Revised priors restore effective shrinkage in edge partition models, with an infinite variant showing strong predictive and inference performance.

paragraphs: A low-rank matrix can encode useful structure even when its observed entries are noisy, missing, or corrupted. This paper studies reconstructing that underlying matrix from the singular values and singular vectors of the contaminated observation. The challenge is separating recoverable structure from the effects of contamination.

The authors place several common contamination models into one framework, including arbitrary combinations of the considered noise, missing-value, outlier, and corrupt-entry models. They then derive an algorithm that estimates the original matrix by changing the observed singular values. The algorithm is asymptotically optimal and applies across the contamination models covered by the analysis.

The paper also identifies an explicit signal-to-noise threshold below which estimation from the observed matrix's singular value decomposition must fail in a specified sense. This pairs an estimation procedure with a boundary on what that information can support. The result concerns the stated decomposition-based recovery setting, and its optimality is asymptotic rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every finite matrix.
neurips-2017-optimal-shrinkage-of-singul.tldr: A unified contamination framework yields asymptotically optimal singular-value shrinkage and a signal-to-noise cutoff for decomposition-based recovery.

paragraphs: Gated recurrent units model time-series data and are commonly trained with gradient-based optimization. Their gradients can sometimes increase sharply, disrupting learning. This paper examines that problem through the dynamics of the recurrent model: a small change in parameters can trigger an abrupt change in how the GRU behaves over time.

The authors identify a condition under which such a drastic dynamical change occurs. They use that analysis to design a learning method that constrains the GRU's dynamics, aiming to keep parameter updates from producing those abrupt transitions. The proposed intervention therefore acts on the behavior associated with the gradient explosion.

Experiments evaluate the method on language modeling and polyphonic music modeling. The authors report that it can prevent exploding gradients and improve modeling accuracy in those evaluations. These findings connect training stability with predictive performance: controlling the identified dynamical behavior helped both in the tested tasks. The abstract presents experimental support for this effect rather than a claim that every possible GRU training run is protected.
neurips-2017-preventing-gradient-explosi.tldr: Constraining GRU dynamics can prevent gradient explosions and improve accuracy, as shown in language and music modeling experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting where two proteins interact requires identifying which amino acid residue pairs belong to their interface. This paper approaches that task with graph convolutional networks, using graphs that represent protein three-dimensional structure. The application matters for understanding interfaces relevant to drug discovery and design.

The authors examine both existing and newly proposed spatial graph convolution operators. Each convolution processes a node's local neighborhood, and stacking layers allows learned representations to integrate information across the protein graph. A further architecture combines the learned features from two proteins to classify residue pairs as interface members or nonmembers.

This design connects structural representation learning to the pairwise prediction required by the task. Rather than treating the protein representations as the final output, it uses them jointly to make decisions about contacts between proteins. In experiments, several graph convolution operators achieve higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art SVM method considered for this task. The reported result supports multiple operators within the evaluated protein-interface prediction setting.
neurips-2017-protein-interface-predictio.tldr: Graph convolutions learn protein structure features that improve residue-pair interface prediction over the evaluated SVM method.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs perceived faces from measured brain responses by combining probabilistic inference with deep learning. It divides reconstruction into two linked inverse problems: recovering latent features from brain activity and then recovering an image from those features. The latent representation provides the connection between neural measurements and visual content.

The first stage reverses a linear transformation from latent features to brain responses using maximum a posteriori estimation. This selects a feature estimate through probabilistic inference. The second stage reverses the nonlinear transformation from a perceived stimulus to its latent features, using convolutional neural networks trained through an adversarial approach.

The authors test the combined method in a functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment and report state-of-the-art reconstructions of perceived faces. The finding supports the complete decoding pipeline in that experimental setting. Its methodological significance is the division of labor between a probabilistic estimate of the hidden representation and a learned nonlinear reconstruction stage, allowing each part of the brain-to-image mapping to be addressed separately.
neurips-2017-reconstructing-perceived-fa.tldr: Probabilistic latent-feature inference and adversarial convolutional networks reconstruct perceived faces from fMRI responses.

paragraphs: The sound of an object hitting the ground can reveal information about its shape, material, and falling height. This paper builds a system that infers those properties from audio. Its approach begins with an efficient physics-based simulation engine that represents knowledge about how physical events produce sound.

Inference follows an analysis-by-synthesis strategy: the system uses synthesis to reason about object properties that could explain the observed sound. To accelerate this process, the authors learn a direct mapping from sound waves to object properties. Those predictions initialize the inference procedure, giving it an informed starting point while retaining the simulation-based reasoning stage.

The model performs well on synthetic clips and real recordings without requiring annotated data. Behavioral studies compare its estimates with human responses for shape, material, and falling height, and the authors report near-human performance. The result supports combining physical simulation with learned initialization for the tested acoustic inference tasks. The learned mapping contributes speed by guiding where the subsequent inference begins.
neurips-2017-shape-and-material-from-sou.tldr: Physics-based inference with learned initialization estimates falling objects' properties from sound, achieving reported near-human performance without annotated data.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process approximations use a limited collection of pseudo-points to make probabilistic modeling practical for larger datasets. Streaming data adds another requirement: as observations arrive, the model must update both its beliefs about function values and the hyperparameters governing its behavior.

The paper identifies shortcomings in existing streaming approaches, including hand-designed hyperparameter updates, catastrophic forgetting, and slow incorporation of new data. It develops a principled framework for streaming Gaussian process models that includes hyperparameter learning and optimization of pseudo-input locations. The approximation's support locations can therefore be adjusted alongside the model settings as learning proceeds.

This addresses more than updating predictions with an otherwise fixed model. The framework brings the posterior, hyperparameters, and pseudo-input choices into the streaming learning problem, connecting uncertainty updates with adaptation of the sparse representation. The authors assess the framework on synthetic and real-world datasets. The abstract establishes the scope of that evaluation but does not state a particular performance margin or a universal elimination of the earlier methods' difficulties.
neurips-2017-streaming-sparse-gaussian-p.tldr: A streaming sparse Gaussian process framework supports online posterior updates, hyperparameter learning, and pseudo-input optimization.

paragraphs: Measurements of multiple features across multiple individuals and times naturally form a three-dimensional tensor. This paper asks how to find a subset of individuals and a subset of features whose time trajectories share a low-dimensional structure. The grouping is therefore based on coordinated behavior over time.

The formulation allows trajectories to have different scales across individuals or features while remaining in the same low-dimensional subspace. That makes similarity more flexible than requiring matching signal magnitudes. The authors study the information-theoretic limits of recovering this structure under a generative model, addressing what the available observations can support in principle.

They also propose an efficient spectral algorithm and analyze an achievability bound in an asymptotic regime. This gives a theoretical account of conditions under which their method can solve the problem, alongside the broader information limit. Experiments on several synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's efficiency. The contribution joins a structured definition of temporal biclustering with computational and statistical analysis.
neurips-2017-tensor-biclustering-8df41e2.tldr: Tensor biclustering finds subsets of individuals and features with shared low-dimensional time dynamics, using an efficient spectral method.

paragraphs: A language model may encounter text whose distribution differs from what it previously learned. Continuous cache models help adapt predictions using recent context, but earlier versions cover only a limited history. This paper extends that approach so adaptation can draw on a much larger collection of past representations.

The proposed memory component stores all hidden activations observed in the past. Approximate nearest neighbor search makes it possible to search this large collection efficiently, while quantization supports storage of millions of representations. Together, these techniques make a substantially longer history usable within the cache mechanism.

Experiments show significant improvements in the perplexity of pretrained language models on new distributions, indicating better predictive fit in those evaluations. The approach also scales efficiently to contexts much larger than those supported by earlier local caches. The contribution is a practical expansion of the memory available for adaptation: previously computed activations remain accessible beyond a short local window, with search and storage methods supporting the larger scale.
neurips-2017-unbounded-cache-model-for-o.tldr: A large searchable cache of past hidden activations improves language-model adaptation and scales to much longer contexts.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train a sequence classifier without labeled training examples, using statistical patterns in output sequences as a source of guidance. A language model is one example of such information. These patterns can be obtained independently of the input data, potentially making them inexpensive or free even when labeling the training inputs would be costly.

The authors propose a training objective for this setting and investigate its properties. Compared with earlier approaches, it is less prone to getting trapped in trivial solutions and does not require a strong generative model. These properties matter because avoiding uninformative solutions is part of making learning without labels useful. The claim is a reduced tendency toward such solutions, rather than a guarantee that they cannot occur.

The objective is harder to optimize in its functional form, so the authors develop a stochastic primal-dual gradient method to solve it effectively. On real-world datasets, the approach produces substantially lower errors than the other baseline methods tested. Its test errors are nevertheless about twice those of fully supervised learning. The findings therefore show a substantial improvement among the compared unsupervised methods, with a remaining performance gap relative to training with labels.
neurips-2017-unsupervised-sequence-class.tldr: Output-sequence statistics enable classifier training without labels, substantially improving on tested unsupervised baselines while yielding about twice the test error of fully supervised learning.

paragraphs: Point processes model sequences of events occurring at irregular times. Many practical models describe them through a parametrized intensity function. This paper argues that restrictive choices for that function can limit expressiveness, while maximum-likelihood training can struggle with sequence distributions that have multiple distinct modes.

The proposed approach generates a target point process by transforming nuisance processes, avoiding an explicit intensity-based formulation. Training also avoids likelihood evaluation and instead uses Wasserstein distance between point processes. The model construction and training objective therefore address separate aspects of the problem: how event sequences are represented and how generated behavior is compared with the target.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report better performance than conventional point process models. These results support the proposed combination in the evaluated settings. The contribution is an alternative route to learning event-sequence distributions, coupling a generative transformation with a distributional distance rather than relying on the practical intensity parametrizations and likelihood training criticized in the paper.
neurips-2017-wasserstein-learning-of-dee.tldr: An intensity-free generative point process model learns through Wasserstein distance and outperforms conventional models in the reported experiments.
